title: GATE: Go toolchain upgraded before goretrotv.demosrv.uk is published
description:
A PRECONDITION OF PUBLICATION, not a nice-to-have. Carried from the phase 1 security audit (plan/security-audit-phase-1.md, section 3), whose reachability triage changed what the numbers mean.

THE FACT THAT CHANGES THE DECISION. govulncheck reports 29 standard-library vulnerabilities this tree CALLS. Four of them are fixable within the Go 1.22 line. The auditor triaged all 29 by REACHABILITY FROM ATTACKER-CONTROLLED BYTES rather than by static call-graph 'called', and the result inverts the obvious reading:

- 6 IDs execute on attacker bytes AT THE LISTENER -- GO-2026-3563 (chunked request smuggling), 6089 (h2c preface timeout), 5039, 4601/4010 -- plus 1 more reachable only with pprof enabled (4341, via pprof.Profile -> FormValue).
- The other 22 are TLS/x509/DNS/OS machinery this program never enters.
- **ALL FOUR of the 1.22-fixable IDs fall in the UNREACHABLE buckets. Every single wire-path ID needs Go >= 1.23.8.**

So the patch bump from 1.22.2 to 1.22.12 that looked like the actionable mitigation buys NOTHING on any path an attacker can reach. It is worth doing for hygiene; it is not a security answer. The only real answer is a newer toolchain.

WHY THIS BELONGS TO PHASE 5 SPECIFICALLY. Today nothing is published: the listener binds loopback, the stack is not running, and those 6 wire-path IDs have no wire. Phase 5 is the phase that puts an HTTP surface on a public host at goretrotv.demosrv.uk behind Traefik. THAT is the moment the reachable six stop being theoretical. Publishing on Go 1.22 means publishing with six known, called, attacker-reachable standard-library vulnerabilities and no patch available in the line.

WHAT TO DO: upgrade the host and CI to a Go the wire-path IDs are fixed in (>= 1.23.8; prefer current stable), rebuild the baseline from the OLDEST toolchain then in use so it stays a superset, and confirm the reachable six leave the called set. NOTE the host constraint recorded in docs/decisions/0001-scaffold.md: this machine cannot fetch a toolchain (dl.google.com unreachable) and its Go comes from the distro, so this needs action outside the sandbox -- which is exactly why it is a gate rather than a task someone can quietly skip.

ALSO RECOMMENDED by the auditor, cheap and separate: move the reachability triage table INTO tools/govulncheck-baseline.txt. Today --write-baseline rewrites the ID list wholesale with no per-entry reason, so the file cannot say WHY each entry is accepted -- and an accepted-vulnerability list that does not record its reasoning is one nobody can re-audit.

Blocks gort-4sx.5 (production Dockerfile/Traefik/TLS) and gort-4sx.6 (developer surfaces must not be published).
source: plan/security-audit-phase-1.md; gort-6ar.13; gort-6ar.21

title: The Go emitter must never sample between a branch and its delay slot (carried from phase 1)
description:
CARRIED FROM PHASE 1 as a design constraint with NO COMMITTED ENFORCEMENT. Surfaced by p1-qa auditing TC-1.6, settled by p1-core in commit 5c02f82 ('The straddle becomes a POSITIVE test, and the port is the side that conforms'), and recorded here because phase 1 had no CPU to enforce it against.

THE CONSTRAINT. The oracle retires a branch AND its delay slot in one loop iteration, so it steps over the checkpoint boundary: 477 of 4,629 checkpoints on the recorded cold boot land off-boundary (about one in ten), the first at its FOURTH checkpoint. THE PORT IS THE SIDE THAT CONFORMS -- the oracle is the reference and editing it to agree with the port is the move that destroys its value. So the Go emitter must observe at the same instants the oracle does, and must NEVER sample mid-pair.

WHY MID-PAIR IS NOT MERELY DIFFERENT BUT WRONG: between a branch and its delay slot the machine state is incomplete -- the pending branch target and the MIPS16 delay flag are not folded into the hash. A hash taken there does not describe a state either implementation can be at. This is the same rule the interrupt path already follows.

WHAT HAPPENS IF THIS IS GOT WRONG: oraclecmp no longer STOPS on such a window (that was gort-6ar.26, fixed), but it still cannot compare it -- it counts it, names it and carries on. So a port that samples mid-pair does not fail loudly; it quietly makes a growing fraction of the boot incomparable, and FR-6's coverage erodes without any gate going red. On the recorded boot that would be one window in ten, invisible.

WHERE IT BITES: TASK-2.2 (the instruction loop) and TASK-2.9 (drive the first divergence to zero). TASK-2.9 in particular cannot mean anything if the two sides sample differently -- its whole premise is that a remaining divergence is a CPU defect rather than a sampling artefact.

WHAT TO BUILD: a committed check that the Go emitter's checkpoint icounts are reachable sampling points, not mid-pair. The cheapest form is asserting that no checkpoint is emitted while a branch is pending. WATCH IT FAIL: sample deliberately mid-pair and confirm the check goes red, then restore -- and per the phase's own hard-won rule, the control must fire on an input the real loop can produce and against a value the test environment does not supply for free.

source: plan/test-plan-phase-1.md TC-1.6; gort-6ar.26; commit 5c02f82

title: The two emitters sample at different instants, so a live oracle-vs-Go comparison dies at checkpoint 4
description:
FOUND BY p1-qa, CONFIRMED BY THE LEAD IN THE CODE. This is the one that stops FR-6 doing its job, and it is upstream of oraclecmp rather than in it.

THE FACT. The real oracle stream has 478 of 4,934 checkpoints landing OFF-BOUNDARY (300001, 1000001, 1500001, ...) -- about 10%, and the FIRST is at the 4th checkpoint. The MIPS32 path retires a branch and its delay slot in one loop iteration and steps over the interval boundary.

THE BEHAVIOUR. compare.go pairs by WINDOW correctly (no WindowMissing). But having paired, compare.go:191 does 'if ca.ICount != cb.ICount -> CadenceDiverged' and RETURNS BEFORE COMPARING HASHES. Verified with a synthetic straddle carrying IDENTICAL hashes (300000 vs 300001): exit 1, 'cadence diverged at window 3 ... go reached instruction 300000, oracle reached 300001'.

THE CONTRADICTION. compare.go:114's own doc comment says demanding equal instruction counts 'would report a divergence at the first straddling branch between two machines that agree perfectly'. The code does exactly that, one scope inward. TestADifferentInstructionCountInTheSameWindowIsItsOwnKindOfDivergence pins the behaviour, so the test enshrines it.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND PHASE 1. On a live oracle-vs-Go run, oraclecmp exits 1 at checkpoint 4 and NEVER REACHES a state comparison. So gort-6ar.25's committed live comparison cannot mean anything, and phase 2's 'drive the first divergence to zero' has no instrument to drive. FR-6 is the project's only independent correctness check and it is currently unable to compare the two machines at all.

THE DIAGNOSIS IS THE VALUABLE PART, and it is p1-qa's: THE COMPARATOR IS HONEST. A hash taken after 300,001 instructions is not comparable to one taken after 300,000, so 'cadence diverged' is the truthful answer GIVEN THOSE INPUTS. No comparator can rescue it. The defect is that the two emitters SAMPLE AT DIFFERENT INSTANTS.

REJECTED FIX: making oraclecmp tolerate a +1 skew. That compares different instants and calls it agreement -- it would turn the project's only independent check into one that cannot see a real one-instruction divergence. p1-qa refused to tick it on that basis and is right.

THE TWO REAL OPTIONS, for p1-core to choose and justify:
(a) The ORACLE samples at the exact boundary -- hash before retiring the delay slot when the branch crosses it.
(b) The GO side adopts the oracle's retirement granularity, so both land on the same instants.

GOVERNING CONSTRAINT: the oracle is the REFERENCE and the port conforms to it (CLAUDE.md: editing the oracle to agree with the Go port is the one move that destroys its value). That points at (b). If (a) is nonetheless correct -- and it may be, since stopping between a branch and its delay slot is a legitimate architectural state with the BD bit set, so sampling there is defensible as making the instrument sample at a DEFINED point rather than as making it agree -- then it must be argued on that ground, and proved inert against existing probes exactly as TASK-1.9 was (before/after baseline, anchored on figures the record states independently).

Whichever is chosen, the fix must make the straddle case a POSITIVE test: two agreeing machines that straddle a boundary must compare EQUAL, not merely fail differently.

BLOCKS gort-6ar.25 (the committed live comparison) and should be resolved before phase 2 (gort-dji) starts its divergence work.

OWNERSHIP: p1-core -- internal/platform/statehash, cmd/oraclecmp, reference/digibox-boot.html.
agent: /go-engineer
close_reason: Fixed (commit 0f2dc1f). The comparison no longer returns at the first window where the instruction counts differ: it counts such windows, notes them, and carries on, reporting BOTH the first disagreement of any kind AND the first window where both reached the same instruction count and their states differed. Hashes are still NOT compared across different instants - that would manufacture a false finding - but that no longer stops the instrument. oraclecmp prints both, says how many windows were incomparable and why, and points tier 2 at the STATE divergence rather than at the straddle. Proved on the real recorded boot: a simulated port stream with all 477 off-boundary checkpoints moved onto their boundaries plus one genuine state difference at instruction 200,000,000 now reports the straddle at window 3 AND finds the state divergence at window 2000, 4,151 windows agreed, 477 named incomparable; before it stopped at window 3. Four mutations each watched, including returning at the first straddle (the shipped bug itself) - note one mutation attempt was a no-op because 'break' inside a 'switch' breaks the switch, and it SURVIVED until the mutation was fixed. Compared now counts the whole shared range rather than the prefix, because stopping early made that number mean 'agreed before I stopped looking'. The emitter gains the upstream contract as documentation: both sides must sample at the same instant, never between a branch and its delay slot - the same rule the interrupt path follows, and the state mid-pair is not well defined since the pending branch target is not in the hash. Also fixed two tests that were passing on luck: TC-1.6's injected corruption was an XOR applied every instruction (toggling back and forth) and then an OR that was a no-op; it now writes COP0 12, which the toy program never touches.

title: GATE: phase 1 verified against the RUNNING stack, on the REAL firmware
description:
Not a suite. The binary is built and RUN on this machine, against the real, uncurated firmware images in firmware/ (FLASH_U202.bin, FLASH_U203.bin) -- not a fixture, not a synthesised ROM.

Close only when ALL of these have been OBSERVED, each with the command and its output quoted in the close reason:
1. ./ctl.sh up (or the documented run command) starts the binary and the health endpoint answers.
2. The firmware loader loads the REAL 2 MB flash images and verifies them against firmware/MANIFEST.md checksums. A deliberately corrupted copy is REFUSED, naming the mismatch.
3. A real checkpoint stream is emitted from a real run -- a non-empty file with a plausible checkpoint count -- and oraclecmp reports agreement/divergence over it, NOT over an empty or truncated stream.
4. The boot gate has been SEEN to go red against a deliberately broken build, and green again afterwards.
5. Developer surfaces (health/instrument endpoints) are confirmed bound to 127.0.0.1 and NOT reachable on the host's LAN address -- checked with a real connection attempt, not by reading the source.

Assert the OUTCOME, never the absence of an exception. A clean exit code over an empty artefact is the failure mode this gate exists to catch.

title: A forged member count in an aggregate snapshot kills the process unrecoverably (audit M-2)
description:
SECURITY AUDIT FINDING M-2 (plan/security-audit-phase-1.md), proved not theorised. This one is filed rather than carried because it BREAKS A RECORDED ARCHITECTURE DECISION.

THE BUG. internal/platform/snapcodec/set.go:136 does 'names := make([]string, 0, count)' where count is the blob's OWN uint32 claim, allocated BEFORE any check that the payload could hold that many members.

THE PROOF. A well-formed one-member container from the real SetWriter, count field overwritten to 0xFFFFFFFF, fed to OpenSet via a go test -overlay probe (nothing written into the tree) under ulimit -v 8000000: 'runtime: out of memory: cannot allocate 68719476736-byte block ... fatal error: out of memory', frame snapcodec.OpenSet set.go:136. On a host with generous overcommit the same input instead commits 64 GB of address space and reads as a HANG.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SEVERITY SUGGESTS. This is a runtime THROW, not a panic -- NO recover() ANYWHERE CAN CATCH IT. So it bypasses both the httpx Recover middleware and the architecture rule in CLAUDE.md: 'Errors are values; a bad guest instruction halts visibly. It must never take the process down or, worse, continue plausibly.' A malformed snapshot currently takes the process down, which is the one outcome that decision forbids.

AND IT IS A SHARED PRIMITIVE. Every phase-4 restore path and every replay/oracle comparison inherits it. Today a snapshot is an operator-supplied file (SPEC FR-8) with no network ingress, which is why the audit rated it Medium rather than High -- but the input becomes less trusted the moment snapshots are exchanged, and the failure is total.

NOT A BUG NEXT DOOR: bus.decodeSnapshot (internal/bus/snapshot.go:179) gets this right -- it uses an unsized map. Reader.Words (snapcodec.go:362) also gets it right, checking remaining() first. OpenSet is the one that does not, which is why a single consistent guard is the fix rather than a style preference.

FIX (one line, plus its test): drop the capacity hint, or guard as Words does -- each member costs at least 8 bytes (two length prefixes), so refuse when uint64(count)*8 > uint64(r.remaining()), naming the claimed count and the bytes remaining. Add the forged-count case to set_test.go beside TestAHeaderCountThatDisagreesWithItsContentsIsRefused.

WATCH IT FAIL FIRST: reproduce the OOM with the forged count before fixing, then confirm the guard turns it into a named refusal. The phase rule applies -- the control must fire on an input the real system can actually produce, and a forged uint32 in a file is exactly that.

OWNER: p1-platform (snapcodec is its package).
agent: /go-engineer
close_reason:
Commit b02b06d. The finding is correct and the severity argument is right: this outranks its Medium rating because it breaks a recorded architecture decision, not merely because it crashes.

REPRODUCED BEFORE FIXING, from an input the real system can actually carry — a genuine one-member container with its count field overwritten to 0xFFFFFFFF, which is what a corrupt or hostile snapshot file contains. Built the probe through `go test -overlay` so the shared tree was never touched, and ran it under `ulimit -v 4000000`:

    runtime: out of memory: cannot allocate 68719476736-byte block (3833856 in use)
    fatal error: out of memory
    runtime.throw(...)
    runtime.makeslice(...)
    snapcodec.OpenSet(...) set.go:136

A FORTY-BYTE BLOB. The stack confirms the lead's severity argument precisely: the frame is runtime.throw, not a panic, so no recover() anywhere can catch it — it goes past httpx.Recover and takes the process down. That is the one outcome "errors are values; a bad guest instruction halts visibly; it must never take the process down or, worse, continue plausibly" forbids. And on a host with generous overcommit it would not even fail loudly: it commits 64 GB of address space and reads as a hang.

THE FIX. Every member costs at least eight payload bytes — a four-byte length prefix for its name and another for its blob — so a container claiming more members than remaining/8 is describing a payload that is not there, and the claim is checked before anything is sized from it. The same forged blob now returns: "snapcodec: machine: snapshot blob is truncated: header claims 4294967295 members, which need at least 34359738360 payload bytes, and 15 remain". ErrTruncated is the honest sentinel: from the reader's side a forged count and a genuinely truncated blob are the same statement — the header claims more than is present.

The comparison widens to int64 rather than uint64, so both conversions are widening and cannot misrepresent their input. The largest product possible here (0xFFFFFFFF members at eight bytes, about 34 billion) fits int64 with room to spare, whereas an unsigned comparison would need remaining() proved non-negative first — a second thing to get right for no benefit. That also cleared a real gosec G115 finding rather than suppressing it.

THE GUARD SHADOWED ANOTHER ONE, and I caught it because this phase has now taught me to look. Two cases in TestAHeaderCountThatDisagreesWithItsContentsIsRefused previously surfaced as ErrShortRead and are now caught earlier by the count check; their expectations are updated, and — the important half — the short-read path gets a case of its OWN rather than being left unexercised behind the new check. It is still reachable whenever a plausible count contains a lying member length, so TestAMemberWhoseOwnLengthRunsOffTheEndIsRefused constructs exactly that: one member, enough bytes to be plausible, and a blob length pointing past the end. Without it, fixing this defect would have quietly retired a working guard — which is the same defect one level up.

PERMANENT CONTROLS ADDED, both firing on inputs the real system can produce: TestAForgedMemberCountIsRefusedBeforeAnythingIsAllocated does the byte-level overwrite of a real container (and asserts the error NAMES the claimed count and the writer, because "it returned an error" would also be satisfied by the reader running off the end a moment later — a different failure that looks the same from outside), and TestAMemberCountLargerThanThePayloadCouldHoldIsRefused covers the range including the boundary of one member too many.

MUTANT: removing the guard kills the suite by reproducing the original OOM at set.go:160 — run under a memory limit so that proving it could not thrash the host. A violent kill, but the right one: the mutant's failure IS the fault the guard prevents.

CHECKS: gofmt clean, go vet ./... exit 0, go test -race ./... exit 0 across 14 packages — including internal/bus, which consumes this container and whose own refusal tests pass unchanged — golangci-lint 0 issues, ./ctl.sh gate green. No probe file was left in the tree; it existed only as an overlay.

title: The boot gate's 'names the build' stage cannot fail for its stated reason
description:
FOUND BY THE LEAD while driving ./ctl.sh gate independently. The stage passes against exactly the binary it exists to reject, on every run.

THE EVIDENCE. A green run prints: 'ok  health names the build  version=dev commit=unknown'. 'dev' and 'unknown' are the LINKER DEFAULTS from internal/version -- they are what a binary reports when nobody told it what it is. That is the definition of unidentifiable, and the stage calls it ok.

WHY IT CANNOT FAIL. tools/boot-gate.sh:105 builds with a bare 'go build -o "/goretrotv" ./cmd/goretrotv' -- NO -ldflags, unlike the Makefile which injects Version/Commit/Date. So the binary under test can ONLY ever report dev/unknown. Line 170 then asserts merely '[[ -n "" && -n "" ]]' -- non-empty. Both placeholders are non-empty, so the assertion is satisfied by construction. The only route to a failure is the 'not reached' path, which is a different stage's failure wearing this stage's label.

THE NEGATIVE CONTROL FIRED ON A FAULT THE REAL SYSTEM CANNOT EXHIBIT. The stage WAS watched going red -- against a stub build returning an EMPTY version. But the real build path cannot produce an empty version; it produces 'dev'. So the control proved the assertion works on an input that will never occur, while the input that does occur passes. This is precisely the shape p1-qa was briefed to hunt: 'a negative control whose subject cannot actually exhibit the fault'.

WHY THE STAGE IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN DELETING. Its stated rationale is right and is the project's own: a gate that passes against a binary nobody can identify has proved nothing about the tree it was checking. The same defect was found and fixed EARLIER IN THIS PHASE in ctl.sh -- 'cmd_up' was letting compose default to VERSION=dev/COMMIT=unknown, and export_build_args was added precisely so /health would name the real build. The gate reintroduced it one layer down.

THE FIX:
1. Build with the same -ldflags the Makefile uses, so the binary under test carries a real version, commit and date. Reusing the Makefile's target is better than copying the flags: two definitions of the build identity is the duplication this project keeps paying for.
2. Assert IDENTIFIABILITY, not non-emptiness. The commit reported by /health should match the tree the gate is running against -- compare it to 'git rev-parse --short HEAD'. That is a claim that can actually be false.
3. WATCH IT FAIL ON THE REAL PATH: build without ldflags on purpose, confirm the stage goes red naming dev/unknown, then restore. A control that fires only on a synthetic input is the thing being fixed here, so the new control must fire on the input the system really produces.

OWNERSHIP: p1-platform -- tools/boot-gate.sh and ctl.sh are its files.
BLOCKS gort-6ar.17, which cannot honestly report the running stack verified while one of its stages is decorative.

Commit 23382d8. The finding is correct and the diagnosis was exact: the stage passed against precisely the binary it existed to reject, on every run.

ROOT CAUSE, confirmed by reading rather than assumed: tools/boot-gate.sh built with a bare `go build` and no -ldflags, so the binary under test could only ever report the linker defaults from internal/version — `dev` and `unknown`. The assertion was `[[ -n "$version" && -n "$commit" ]]`. Both defaults are non-empty, so it was satisfied by construction, and the only route to red was the "not reached" path, which is a different stage's failure wearing this stage's label.

AND THE NEGATIVE CONTROL WAS THE REAL DEFECT. The stage WAS watched going red — against a stub returning an EMPTY version. The real build path cannot produce an empty version; it produces `dev`. So the control proved the assertion against a fault the system cannot exhibit, while the input that occurs on every single run passed. That is the exact shape p1-qa was briefed to hunt, and I built it into my own gate while writing negative controls for everything else.

FIX 1 — ONE DEFINITION OF THE BUILD IDENTITY. The gate now builds through the Makefile's own `build` target rather than re-implementing it. `build` gained a `BIN_DIR ?= bin` override, defaulting to bin/ so nothing changes for anyone else (verified: bare `make build` still writes goretrotv and oraclecmp to bin/), which lets the gate build into its scratch directory without a second copy of the ldflags existing anywhere. The duplication was the mechanism of the drift, not an incidental detail: the gate re-implemented the build and the re-implementation omitted the stamping.

FIX 2 — ASSERT IDENTITY, NOT NON-EMPTINESS. /health's commit must equal `git rev-parse --short HEAD`. That is a claim that can actually be false, and it is false the moment the stamping stops happening. It also answers the question that matters when a divergence turns up weeks later — was that binary built from this tree? — which is the same doubt that put oraclecmp in the image alongside the emulator. If HEAD cannot be determined at all the stage FAILS rather than passing, because an identity claim that cannot be checked is not granted.

WATCHED FAILING ON THE REAL PATH, which is the entire point of the fix rather than a formality:
- The real cmd/goretrotv, built exactly as the old gate built it (bare `go build`, no ldflags). This binary USED TO PASS this stage. It now fails it, ALONE — 1 of 5, with the other four stages green — which is what shows the stage is independently falsifiable rather than collapsing together with its neighbours. Message: "reports commit='unknown', this tree is 6e553e2 — those are the linker defaults, so the build was not stamped".
- A correctly stamped binary from a DIFFERENT commit: refused by name, "reports commit='da71a6e', this tree is 6e553e2". This is the version-skew case.
- A HALF-stamped binary (commit stamped to HEAD, version left at the default): refused as "half-stamped". I tested this branch specifically because it would otherwise have shipped unproven — the same dead-code-versus-missing-test discipline applied to my own fix.
- Control, the gate building for itself: green, "version=6e553e2-dirty commit=6e553e2 (matches HEAD)".

ALSO CORRECTED: the gate's own summary line said "The build does not come up" whatever had failed. That is false when the build came up and only the identity claim did not hold. It now reads "FAILED — N of 5 stages. Each FAIL line above says which claim did not hold." A gate's summary has to be as trustworthy as its stages, which is the same standard the stages are held to.

ON THE PATTERN, since the lead named it: this is the second time in the phase that a guard was satisfied by construction, and both times the tell was the same — the control fired on an input the system cannot produce. In snapcodec a surviving mutant meant unreachable code; in internal/oracle two survivors meant one floor shadowing another; here the control itself used a synthetic input. The generalisation is that watching an instrument fail is necessary but not sufficient: it must be watched failing on an input the real system can actually produce. I am recording that here rather than editing the shared library, which remains the lead's call with the user.

description:

Both sides currently fold PC, ISA-as-octet, HI, LO, 32 GPR, 32 COP0 and the RAM digest in the same order -- verified BY READING, which is evidence of intent and not of behaviour.

FIX: once oraclecmp exists (gort-6ar.10), a committed check that compares a real oracle ?cp= stream against a Go stream. That is the artefact that makes TC-1.5's cross-implementation half reproducible instead of remembered.

title: Wire firmware.Load into the startup path so a mismatch refuses the boot
description:
TC-1.4 says 'refuses to START, naming the mismatch'. The loader refuses correctly and is proved at package level (TASK-1.7), but NOTHING CALLS IT: grep confirms firmware.Load appears only in its own tests, and neither cmd/goretrotv nor internal/app references the package. So half of TC-1.4 -- the half the test case actually names -- is unwired, and the phase would have closed with a loader nobody invokes.

Two gaps that are really one:
1. No startup path calls firmware.Load, so a checksum mismatch cannot refuse a boot that never consults it.
2. GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR does not exist in internal/config. p1-core correctly declined to add a config field nothing reads, and nothing reads it because nothing calls Load. Adding both together is what makes either coherent.

SCOPE:
- Add GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR to internal/config. Decide REQUIRED vs defaulted deliberately and state the reasoning: the test to apply is the one used for GORETROTV_ENV -- if a wrong guess means silently running a different ROM, it is required. The completeness test will force it into the committed example file.
- Call firmware.Load on the startup path so a mismatch, a missing image or a wrong size EXITS NON-ZERO naming the problem, before anything else initialises.
- This also closes the latent container trap: the image mounts firmware at /firmware while a relative firmware/ path works only because distroless sets no WORKDIR. Anything that later sets one turns this into a wrong-or-absent ROM, which is TC-1.4's own subject arriving through the back door.

- Built binary, real firmware present -> starts.
- Built binary, one image corrupted -> exits non-zero naming the file and the digest mismatch.
- Built binary, firmware dir absent/empty -> exits non-zero naming what is missing.
- Assert the OUTCOME, not the absence of an exception: confirm the process did NOT reach 'listening'.

CARRIED FROM PHASE 1 SECURITY AUDIT, finding M-1 (plan/security-audit-phase-1.md section 2). The audit PROVED the loopback negative -- no code path builds a listener from anything but the audited config value, the default is loopback and tested, pprof does not widen it -- BUT with one limit that is exactly this rule's job:

THE CONTROL IS A DEFAULT PLUS PROSE, NOT AN INVARIANT. internal/config/config.go:55 (field) and :184-213 (assign stores string fields verbatim) accept ANY interface with no refusal. Demonstrated live by the audit: GORETROTV_HTTP_ADDR=:8099 is honoured silently. With GORETROTV_ENABLE_PPROF=true also set, pprof (heap and goroutine dumps, cmdline, CPU profiles -- a CPU-burn DoS lever) lands on a public interface. Two operator mistakes are needed TODAY; ONE will do once phase 4 lands, because the gdb stub -- arbitrary read/write of the emulated machine -- arrives with no bind of its own and inherits this address.

THE FIX THE AUDIT RECOMMENDS, which is what makes ARCH-DEV-1 a real check rather than an aspiration:
1. Add a bool config field AllowNonLoopbackBind with env tag GORETROTV_BIND_ALL_INTERFACES, defaulting false.
2. In config.Load, after assign, parse HTTPAddr with net.SplitHostPort and REFUSE when the host is empty, 0.0.0.0, :: or any non-loopback IP, unless that flag is set -- naming CLAUDE.md's rule in the error text.
3. Set the flag as a LITERAL in docker-compose.yml beside the container's GORETROTV_HTTP_ADDR of :8099. The container legitimately needs the widening; its loopback-only port mapping is the fence.
4. Document the variable in the committed example env file -- the config completeness test will demand it.

ARCH-DEV-1 then becomes greppable: the ONLY setter of GORETROTV_BIND_ALL_INTERFACES in the tree is docker-compose.yml, and a second setter anywhere fails the rule. That is a probe that can actually go red.

title: Add govulncheck to CI, pinned to a version that builds under Go 1.22
description:

Commit 14d37f6. tools/vulncheck.sh + tools/govulncheck-baseline.txt, a `vulnerabilities` job in CI, and ctl.sh/Makefile wired to the same script so `./ctl.sh vuln` and `make vuln` cannot drift apart.

THE FINDING THAT SHAPED THE TASK, and it is worth escalating rather than burying: govulncheck reports 29 vulnerabilities THIS TREE ACTUALLY CALLS, all in the standard library, and 25 of them are fixed only in Go 1.23 or later. ADR 0001 records that no external dependencies makes the stdlib the entire supply-chain surface; what it did not anticipate is that the surface is EOL and unpatchable here. Four of the 29 are fixable within the 1.22 line (1.22.3/1.22.4/1.22.11/1.22.12); the remaining 25 need a toolchain this host cannot fetch. THE REAL FIX IS A NEWER GO, and this gate is a way of living with that honestly rather than a substitute for it.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE GATE'S SHAPE: a plain `govulncheck ./...` step would be red on every run for ever, with nothing any committer could do about it. That is not strictness; it is a gate people stop reading — the same decoration failure as a permanently green one, arrived at from the other side. So the gate asks the answerable question: is there anything NEW? Anything not in the committed baseline fails. A baseline entry no longer reported is PRINTED but does not fail, because the exact set varies with the 1.22.x patch level and failing on it would be unactionable — the same reasoning that scoped the pre-commit hook to the packages being committed.

THE PIN WAS WRONG ON FIRST ATTEMPT AND I CAUGHT IT BY TESTING: the issue title says "pinned to a version that builds under Go 1.22", and the locally installed govulncheck v1.3.0 reports `Go: go1.22.2`, which looks like confirmation. It is not — that field is the toolchain it ANALYSES with, not the one that built it. `go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@v1.3.0` fails outright: `golang.org/x/vuln@v1.3.0 requires go >= 1.25.0`. Checked the go directive of each candidate and pinned v1.1.4, the newest whose directive is `go >= 1.22.0`. Verified it installs and runs under Go 1.22 locally AND on the CI runner, and that it produces an identical 29-id finding set to v1.3.0, so the baseline is scanner-independent in practice.

PROVED RED THEN GREEN ON THE RUNNER, not merely locally. A scratch branch with one accepted id removed: run 35128961244 FAILED the vulnerabilities job, reporting `25 called, 28 accepted, 1 new` and naming GO-2026-6090 with its advisory URL. Restoring the id gave run 35129103117, GREEN (`25 called, 29 accepted, 0 new`). That exercised the entire path on the runner — installing the pinned scanner under Go 1.22, jq, the scan, the JSON extraction and the comparison. The throwaway PR (#2, draft, DO NOT MERGE) is closed with an explanatory comment, the branch is deleted from origin and locally, the worktree is removed, and `git ls-remote` confirms origin/master is still at f54e9bf.

THE RUNNER VINDICATED THE BASELINE DESIGN BY ACCIDENT, which is the most useful thing the proof produced: it reported 25 called against our 29, because its Go is a newer 1.22.x than this machine's 1.22.2. Generating the baseline from the OLDEST toolchain in use makes it a superset, so a newer patch level reports a subset, produces nothing new, and stays green without anyone pinning patch versions to keep it that way. Had "no longer reported" been a failure, CI would have been red from its very first run for a reason no committer could act on.

FOUR MORE FAILURE PATHS WATCHED LOCALLY, through a `--report` seam that feeds the gate a captured scan (an input override, not a bypass — the comparison is identical either way, and it exists so the gate can be tested without a 30-second scan each time): a new vulnerability -> RED naming it; a baseline that accepts nothing -> RED as a harness failure; an empty report -> RED, because an empty report is not a clean tree; and a report with only unreachable findings -> GREEN, which is correct since nothing is called.

ONE TRAP GUARDED IN A COMMENT because it would silently disarm the gate: with `-format json`, govulncheck EXITS 0 even when it finds vulnerabilities — the exit-3 convention is text-format only. Anyone "simplifying" this to trust the scanner's exit status would produce a gate that always passes. The verdict comes from the comparison; a non-zero status there means the scan itself failed.

Only symbol-level (called) findings are gated. Imported-but-not-called vulnerabilities — 62 of them — are not listed and not gated, because our code has no path to them.

CHECKS: gofmt clean, go vet ./... exit 0, go test -race ./... exit 0 across 13 packages, golangci-lint 0 issues, ./ctl.sh hooks green, bash -n clean on both scripts. p1-core's in-flight Dockerfile, cmd/oraclecmp/ and statehash files were verified absent from the staged set.
